l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Israel's chosen men, thirty thousand, accompany David, and all the house of Israel plays instruments before the LORD. They bring up the ark with shouting and trumpet sound, and the whole multitude, men and women, each receive a portion of bread, dates, and raisins before departing home. David is described as appointed prince over Israel.

l: Zion, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: David's city is where David at first refuses to move the ark after Uzzah's death. The ark is later brought in with joy and celebration and set in the middle of the tent David had pitched for it, where he offers burnt and peace offerings.

l: Uzzah's death, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: Uzzah dies when God strikes him for his error after he grips the ark to steady it as the cattle stumble. David is displeased, names the place Perez Uzzah, and is afraid of the LORD that day, which leads him to leave the ark at Obed-Edom's house.

l: David's dancing, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 6
s: David dances before the LORD with all his might, clothed in a linen ephod, as the ark is brought up with shouting and trumpets. Michal despises it and calls it shameless, but David defends it as celebration before the LORD and says he will be even more undignified.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: King David, settled in his house and at rest from his enemies, tells the prophet Nathan he is troubled that God's ark dwells in curtains while he lives in cedar. Nathan first approves, but that night the LORD tells Nathan to say that he has never asked for a house of cedar, and recalls taking David from the sheep pen to be prince over Israel. The LORD promises to give Israel a settled place and rest from enemies, to make David a house, and to set up David's offspring, who will build a house for his name and whose throne will be established forever. Even if this son sins he will be chastened, but the LORD's loving kindness will not leave him as it left Saul. David sits before the LORD and prays, praising God's greatness, recalling Israel's redemption from Egypt, and asking God to confirm and bless his house forever.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: David, now at rest in his house, observes that he lives in cedar while God's ark is in curtains. The LORD, through Nathan, recalls raising him from the sheep pen to be prince over Israel and promises him a great name, rest from enemies, and a house and throne that will last forever. David responds by sitting before the LORD and praying in humble gratitude.

l: Nathan, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: Nathan the prophet first tells David to do all that is in his heart. That night the LORD's word comes to him, correcting this, and he is sent to deliver the message to David about the house and the promises. He speaks to David all these words according to the vision.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD says he has never lived in a house since bringing Israel out of Egypt, and never asked for one of cedar. He promises David a great name, a place and rest for Israel, a house, and an offspring whose kingdom and throne he will establish forever. He will be a father to that son, chasten him if he sins, and not withdraw his loving kindness as he did from Saul.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD says he will appoint a place for his people Israel, plant them there, and keep them from being moved or afflicted by the children of wickedness as before. In his prayer David describes Israel as a unique nation, redeemed from Egypt and from other nations and their gods, and established as God's people forever.

l: house for God's name (temple), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: David's wish to replace the ark's curtains with a house prompts the LORD's reply that he never asked anyone for a cedar house. The LORD declares that David's offspring will build a house for his name, and he will establish the throne of that son's kingdom forever.

l: David's dynasty (house of David), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD promises that he will make David a house, and that David's house and kingdom will be made sure forever, with his throne established forever. David in his prayer asks God to confirm this promise and bless his house so that it continues forever before him.

l: David's offspring (David's son), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD promises that after David sleeps with his fathers he will set up an offspring from David's own body and establish his kingdom. This son will build a house for the LORD's name, and the LORD will be his father. If he commits iniquity he will be chastened with the rod of men, but the LORD's loving kindness will not depart from him.

l: David's prayer, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 7
s: David sits before the LORD and asks who he is that he has been brought this far, then praises God as great and without equal. He recalls God's redemption of Israel from Egypt, and asks that the word spoken about his house be confirmed forever and that his house be blessed. He says he has found it in his heart to pray because God revealed the promise to him.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 recounts King David's military victories over the Philistines, Moab, Hadadezer king of Zobah, the Syrians of Damascus, and Edom, with the LORD giving him victory wherever he went. David took horsemen, footmen, gold shields, and bronze from Hadadezer, and Toi king of Hamath sent his son Joram with silver, gold, and bronze vessels to bless him. David dedicated the silver and gold from all the subdued nations to the LORD. The chapter closes by noting that David reigned over all Israel with justice and righteousness, and lists his officials: Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, Ahimelech, Seraiah, Benaiah, and David's sons.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: David struck and subdued the Philistines, Moab, Hadadezer, the Syrians of Damascus, and Edom, placing garrisons in Syria and Edom, and the LORD gave him victory wherever he went. He took gold shields and a great quantity of bronze, dedicated silver and gold from all subdued nations to the LORD, and earned a reputation after striking down eighteen thousand Syrians in the Valley of Salt. He reigned over all Israel, executing justice and righteousness for all his people, with Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, Ahimelech, Seraiah, Benaiah, and his own sons serving in his administration.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: David struck the Philistines and subdued them, taking the bridle of the mother city out of their hand. Silver and gold from the Philistines was among the spoils David dedicated to the LORD.

l: Moab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: David defeated Moab and measured them with a line, making them lie on the ground; two lines' worth were put to death and one full line kept alive. The Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.

l: Hadadezer, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: Hadadezer, son of Rehob and king of Zobah, was struck by David as he went to recover his dominion at the River. David took 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 footmen, hamstrung the chariot horses while keeping enough for one hundred chariots, and carried off the gold shields of his servants and much bronze from his cities Betah and Berothai. Toi king of Hamath, who had his own wars with Hadadezer, sent his son Joram to bless David for defeating him.

l: Syrians of Damascus, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: The Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadadezer, and David struck twenty-two thousand of them. David then put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became his servants and brought tribute.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 8
s: David put garrisons throughout all Edom, and all the Edomites became his servants. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: David asks whether anyone remains of Saul's house to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan's sake. Saul's servant Ziba tells him that Jonathan has a lame son, living in the house of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar. David has the son, Mephibosheth, brought to him, assures him he need not fear, promises to restore all of Saul's land, and grants him a permanent place at the king's table. David then instructs Ziba, who has fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm the land for Mephibosheth, and Ziba agrees. Mephibosheth, who has a young son named Mica, lives in Jerusalem and eats at the king's table like one of the king's sons, still lame in both feet.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house so that he may show kindness for Jonathan's sake. He summons Ziba, sends for Mephibosheth, promises to restore Saul's land to him and to have him eat at his table continually, and commands Ziba to farm the land for Mephibosheth.

l: Mephibosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Mephibosheth, son of Jonathan and lame in both feet, is living in Lo Debar in the house of Machir when David sends for him. He falls on his face before David, calls himself a dead dog, receives the promise of Saul's land and a place at the king's table, and then lives in Jerusalem eating there like one of the king's sons. He has a young son named Mica.

l: Ziba, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Ziba is a servant of Saul's house who tells David that Jonathan still has a lame son and where he is. David commands him, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to till Saul's land for Mephibosheth, and Ziba agrees to do as the king commands. His household becomes servants to Mephibosheth.

l: Jonathan, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Jonathan is the reason David seeks to show kindness, and is named as father of Mephibosheth. Ziba reports that he still has a son who is lame in his feet.

l: Saul, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: Saul is named as the grandfather of Mephibosheth and the former owner of the land and possessions that David gives to Mephibosheth. Ziba is described as Saul's servant.

l: Saul’s house, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: David seeks anyone left of Saul's house in order to show kindness. Ziba, a servant of the house, is found, and Mephibosheth is identified as the remaining member; everything belonging to Saul and his house is given to Mephibosheth.

l: land (Mephibosheth and Ziba), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: David promises to restore all of Saul's land to Mephibosheth and declares that all that belonged to Saul and his house is given to him. Ziba, his sons and his servants are to till it and bring in the harvest so that Mephibosheth has bread.

l: kindness, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: David wants to show kindness for Jonathan's sake, which he also calls the kindness of God. He carries it out by restoring Saul's land to Mephibosheth and giving him a continual place at the king's table.

l: king's table, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 9
s: David promises that Mephibosheth will eat bread at his table continually, and this is repeated in the unit. Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem because he eats there continually, like one of the king's sons.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: After the king of the Ammonites dies and his son Hanun takes the throne, David sends servants to comfort Hanun, but Ammonite princes persuade Hanun that they are spies. Hanun shames the servants by shaving half their beards and cutting their garments, and David tells them to wait at Jericho. The Ammonites hire Syrian and other mercenaries, and David sends Joab, who divides the army with his brother Abishai, defeats the Syrians, and sees the Ammonites flee into their city. Hadadezer then brings more Syrians to Helam, where David himself crosses the Jordan, kills many charioteers and horsemen, and strikes down Shobach. The kings serving Hadadezer make peace with Israel, and the Syrians no longer dare help the Ammonites.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: David sent servants to comfort Hanun out of kindness for Hanun's father, and after they were shamed he told them to wait at Jericho. He sent Joab against the Ammonites and Syrians, then personally led all Israel across the Jordan to Helam, where he killed seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen and struck down Shobach.

l: Hanun, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Hanun became king of the Ammonites after his father died. Persuaded by his princes that David's comforters were spies, he shaved half the servants' beards, cut their garments to the buttocks, and sent them away.

l: children of Ammon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: The Ammonite princes convinced Hanun that David's envoys were spies, and the Ammonites, having become odious to David, hired Syrian, Maacah and Tob troops. They drew up at the city gate, but fled into the city before Abishai when the Syrians fled.

l: David's servants, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: David's servants went to the Ammonites to comfort Hanun and were instead humiliated, with half their beards shaved and garments cut off. David sent to meet them and told them to wait at Jericho until their beards grew.

l: Syrians, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: The Syrians of Beth Rehob and Zobah, along with the king of Maacah and the men of Tob, were hired by the Ammonites and fled before Joab. They regrouped under Hadadezer at Helam, were defeated by David, and afterward were afraid to help the Ammonites any more.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Joab was sent by David with the army of mighty men and, seeing the battle set before and behind, took the choicest Israelite men against the Syrians. He urged courage and mutual help, made the Syrians flee, and returned to Jerusalem.

l: Abishai, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Abishai, Joab's brother, was given command of the rest of the people against the Ammonites. Joab promised to help him if the Ammonites proved too strong, and the Ammonites fled before him into the city.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Israel's forces defeated the Syrians twice, first under Joab and then under David at Helam. After the second victory, the kings serving Hadadezer made peace with Israel and served them.

l: Hadadezer, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Hadadezer sent for and brought out the Syrians from beyond the River, who came to Helam under his captain Shobach. After their defeat, the kings who were his servants made peace with Israel and served them.

l: Shobach, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Shobach was the captain of Hadadezer's army and led the Syrians at Helam. David struck him and he died there.

l: battle against Ammon and Syrians, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 10
s: Joab and Abishai fought in two divisions at the Ammonite city gate, with the Syrians in the field, and both enemy forces fled. The Syrians regathered under Hadadezer and were beaten again at Helam by David, ending with peace from Hadadezer's servant kings and Syrian reluctance to aid Ammon.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: While Joab and Israel's army fight the Ammonites and besiege Rabbah, David stays in Jerusalem, sees Bathsheba bathing, summons her, and lies with her. When she tells him she is pregnant, David calls her husband Uriah the Hittite home from the war, hoping he will go to his house, but Uriah refuses to enjoy comfort while the ark and the army are in tents. David then sends a letter to Joab, carried by Uriah himself, ordering that Uriah be placed in the hottest fighting and abandoned so he will die. Joab does so, Uriah dies, and David responds calmly to the news, then marries Bathsheba after her mourning, and she bears him a son. The chapter ends by stating that what David did displeased the LORD.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: David stays in Jerusalem while his army fights, sees Bathsheba, sends for her, and lies with her. After she conceives, he tries to get Uriah to go home, makes him drunk, and finally sends a letter ordering Uriah's death in battle. He then takes Bathsheba as his wife, and what he did displeases the LORD.

l: Bathsheba, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Bathsheba is identified as the daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite, and is described as very beautiful. David takes her and lies with her, she conceives and tells him, and after mourning her husband she becomes David's wife and bears him a son.

l: Uriah the Hittite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Uriah is summoned from the war by David but refuses to go down to his house, saying the ark, Israel, Judah, and Joab's men are camped in the open. He unwittingly carries the letter that orders his death and is killed in the fighting near the city wall.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Joab leads the army against the Ammonites, sends Uriah to David when asked, and on receiving David's letter assigns Uriah to where valiant men are. He then sends a messenger with instructions on how to report Uriah's death to David, and David tells him not to be displeased and to press the attack.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: The LORD is mentioned at the end of the chapter, where it is stated that the thing David had done displeased him.

l: Rabbah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: Rabbah is the city of the Ammonites that Joab and the army besiege. Uriah is killed in fighting near its wall, and David tells Joab to strengthen the battle against the city and overthrow it.

l: letter (David's letter to Joab), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: David writes the letter and sends it to Joab by the hand of Uriah. It instructs Joab to put Uriah at the front of the hottest battle and then retreat from him so that he will be struck down and die.

l: war against Ammon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 11
s: At the time when kings go out, David sends Joab, his servants, and all Israel, who destroy the Ammonites and besiege Rabbah. During the siege, men fall, including David's servants and Uriah, after the men of the city sally out and shoot from the wall.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The LORD sends Nathan to David, and Nathan tells a parable of a rich man who took a poor man's only ewe lamb to feed a traveler. David burns with anger and declares the man deserves to die, and Nathan answers, "You are the man," pronouncing judgment for David's killing of Uriah the Hittite and taking of his wife. David confesses his sin, is told he will not die, but the child born to him will, and after fasting for seven days he sees the child die, then rises, worships, and eats. David comforts Bathsheba, and she bears Solomon, whom the LORD loves and Nathan names Jedidiah. Meanwhile Joab takes Rabbah's royal city and summons David, who captures the city, takes the Ammonite king's crown, and puts the people to forced labor.

l: Nathan, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Nathan is sent by the LORD to David and tells him the parable of the rich man and the poor man's lamb. He then declares "You are the man!", delivers the LORD's judgment, and tells David his sin is put away but the child will die. He later conveys the LORD's naming of Solomon as Jedidiah.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: David is angered by Nathan's parable and pronounces that the rich man deserves to die, only to be told he is that man. He confesses "I have sinned against the LORD," fasts and mourns for the sick child, and after its death worships and eats. He comforts Bathsheba, fathers Solomon, and leads the people to take Rabbah, where he receives the Ammonite king's crown and puts the people to forced labor.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The LORD sends Nathan to David and pronounces judgment through him: the sword will never leave David's house, and evil will rise from his own household. He puts away David's sin so David will not die, strikes the child with sickness, and loves Solomon.

l: rich man (Nathan's parable), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: In Nathan's parable the rich man has very many flocks and herds. When a traveler comes, he spares his own animals and takes the poor man's lamb to prepare for the guest. David declares that this man deserves to die and must restore fourfold.

l: poor man (Nathan's parable), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: In the parable the poor man has nothing but one little ewe lamb that he bought and raised. His lamb is taken by the rich man to feed a traveler.

l: ewe lamb (the poor man's lamb), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The ewe lamb grew up with the poor man and his children, ate his food, drank from his cup, lay in his bosom, and was like a daughter to him. The rich man takes it and prepares it for a traveler.

l: Uriah the Hittite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Uriah the Hittite is named by Nathan as the man David struck with the sword and killed with the sword of the Ammonites, after which David took his wife as his own. This is the basis of the LORD's charge against David.

l: Bathsheba, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Bathsheba, referred to as Uriah's wife and the one David took as his wife, bears David a child who is struck by the LORD and dies. David then comforts her as his wife, lies with her, and she bears Solomon.

l: child (David and Bathsheba's first son), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The child born to David and Uriah's wife is struck by the LORD and becomes very sick, as Nathan foretold. He dies on the seventh day, despite David's fasting and pleading.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Solomon is born to David and Bathsheba after the first child's death. The LORD loves him, and Nathan the prophet is sent to name him Jedidiah for the LORD's sake.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Joab fights against Rabbah and takes the royal city, the city of waters. He sends messengers urging David to gather the rest of the people and take the city himself, lest Joab's name be given to it.

l: Rabbah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Rabbah, the Ammonite city, has its royal city taken by Joab and is then captured by David with all the people. Its king's crown is taken, plunder is carried off, and its people are put to labor.

l: children of Ammon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: The Ammonites are the people whose sword is named as the means by which David had Uriah slain. Their city Rabbah is conquered by David, who takes their king's crown, a talent of gold with precious stones, and puts the people and those of all their cities to forced labor.

l: David's sin (adultery and murder), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: Nathan charges that David despised the LORD's word by killing Uriah the Hittite and taking his wife. The LORD declares the sword will never leave David's house and that his wives will be taken and given to his neighbor publicly. David confesses, and his sin is put away so he will not die, though the child will because it gave the LORD's enemies occasion to blaspheme.

l: David's fasting and mourning for the child, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 12
s: While the child lives, David begs God, fasts, weeps, and lies all night on the ground, refusing the elders' efforts to raise him. After the child dies, he washes, changes clothes, worships in the LORD's house, and eats, explaining that he can't bring the child back but will go to him.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Amnon, son of David, loves his half-sister Tamar, sister of Absalom, and on the advice of his friend Jonadab feigns illness so that David sends Tamar to prepare food for him. Amnon rapes Tamar despite her protests, then hates her and has her thrown out; she mourns publicly and stays desolate in Absalom's house. David is very angry but the text records no action, while Absalom says nothing to Amnon for two years. Absalom then invites the king's sons to a sheep shearing and has his servants kill Amnon when he is merry with wine. Absalom flees to Talmai, king of Geshur, where he stays three years, while Jonadab calms David's fear that all his sons are dead and David mourns Amnon and eventually longs to go out to Absalom.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Absalom tells the wronged Tamar to keep quiet and takes her into his house, then hates Amnon and speaks to him neither good nor bad for two years. He invites the king's sons to a sheep shearing, persuades David to let Amnon come, and commands his servants to kill Amnon when he is merry with wine. He then flees to Talmai, king of Geshur, and stays there three years.

l: Tamar, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Tamar, Absalom's beautiful sister, is sent by David to Amnon's house to make cakes for him. She refuses Amnon's advances, warns of shame and folly, and suggests he ask the king, but he overpowers her and rapes her. After he casts her out and she pleads against it, she puts ashes on her head, tears her robe, and cries aloud, then remains desolate in Absalom's house.

l: Amnon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Amnon, David's son, loves Tamar and becomes sick over her, then follows Jonadab's plan to feign illness and get her sent to him. He rapes her, then hates her more than he had loved her and has his servant bolt her out. Two years later he goes to Absalom's sheep shearing at David's permission and is killed by Absalom's servants.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: David, the king, sends Tamar to Amnon's house at Amnon's request, and is very angry when he hears of the rape, though the text records no action by him. He reluctantly lets Amnon go to Absalom's feast, then tears his garments on hearing a false report that all his sons are dead. He mourns Amnon daily, and in time longs to go out to Absalom, being comforted over Amnon's death.

l: Jonadab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Jonadab, David's nephew and Amnon's friend, is described as a very subtle man. He draws out Amnon's love for Tamar and advises him to feign sickness and ask the king to send her. After the killing he tells David that only Amnon is dead, a result he says Absalom had determined since the rape, and he announces the returning sons.

l: rape of Tamar, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: Amnon forces Tamar after luring her into his room under pretense of illness, ignoring her protest that it is a folly not done in Israel. He then hates her and expels her, which she calls a wrong worse than the first. The act leaves Tamar desolate, angers David, and is the stated reason for Absalom's hatred and Amnon's later death.

l: murder of Amnon, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 13
s: After two full years Absalom has his servants strike down Amnon at a sheep shearing when his heart is merry with wine, while the other sons flee on mules. A false report says all the sons are dead until Jonadab clarifies that only Amnon was killed. It leads to Absalom's flight to Geshur for three years and David's mourning.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Joab, seeing that the king's heart is toward Absalom, sends for a wise woman of Tekoa and instructs her to pose as a long-grieving widow and tell the king a made-up story. She says one of her two sons killed the other in a field and that her family demands the killer's death, which would leave her husband without name or heir. The king promises that not a hair of her son will fall, and she then turns this against him, saying he is guilty for not bringing home his own banished one. The king discerns Joab's hand in it, and she admits Joab put the words in her mouth. The king tells Joab to bring Absalom back from Geshur, but Absalom must live in his own house and not see the king's face. After two years Absalom burns Joab's barley field to force a meeting with Joab, and Joab then takes Absalom's plea to the king, who receives Absalom and kisses him.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Joab perceives the king's heart is toward Absalom and arranges for the woman of Tekoa to speak to the king, putting the words in her mouth. When the king grants the request, Joab thanks him, goes to Geshur, and brings Absalom to Jerusalem. He later ignores Absalom's two summons, has his barley field burned by Absalom's servants, then comes to Absalom and carries his plea to the king.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Absalom is brought back from Geshur to Jerusalem by Joab but is told to live in his own house without seeing the king's face. He is praised for his flawless beauty, has heavy hair weighed at two hundred shekels each year, and has three sons and a daughter named Tamar. After two years he has Joab's field burned to get his attention, says he would rather be dead than kept from the king, and finally bows before the king, who kisses him.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The king hears the woman's story, promises by the LORD's life that not a hair of her son will fall, and then recognizes that Joab is behind it. He orders Joab to bring Absalom back but says Absalom must not see his face. Two years later, after Joab brings Absalom's plea, he calls for Absalom and kisses him.

l: woman of Tekoa, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The woman of Tekoa is a wise woman brought by Joab, who coaches her to dress as a long-time mourner and speak to the king. She tells the story of her two sons, wins the king's oath, and then argues that he is guilty for not bringing home his banished one. When the king asks, she admits Joab sent her and praises the king's wisdom as that of an angel of God.

l: son who killed his brother (widow's son), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: In the woman's story, this son struck his brother in a field with no one to part them and killed him. The family demands his handing over to be killed, which would destroy the heir. The king swears that not a hair of his head will fall to the earth.

l: the widow's story of the two sons, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: The story is a tale Joab put in the woman's mouth: a widow's two sons fought in the field, one killed the other, and the family demands the killer's death, which would quench her last coal and leave her husband no name or remainder. It leads the king to promise protection to the surviving son. The woman then applies it to the king's own situation with his banished son, and the king sees Joab behind it.

l: Absalom's banishment and return, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 14
s: Absalom's banishment in Geshur ends when the king orders Joab to bring him back and Joab brings him to Jerusalem. The return is only partial: Absalom lives in his own house and does not see the king's face for two full years. The matter is resolved when Joab carries Absalom's plea to the king, who calls Absalom in, receives his bow, and kisses him.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Absalom prepares a chariot, horses, and fifty runners, then sits at the city gate intercepting Israelites with lawsuits, promising justice if he were judge and kissing those who bow to him, thereby stealing the hearts of the men of Israel. After forty years he asks King David's permission to go to Hebron to pay a vow, and David sends him in peace. Absalom sends spies through the tribes to proclaim him king at the trumpet sound, takes two hundred unwitting invitees, and summons David's counselor Ahithophel, so the conspiracy grows strong. Warned that Israel's hearts follow Absalom, David flees Jerusalem with his household and servants, leaving ten concubines behind, and Ittai the Gittite pledges loyalty to him. David sends Zadok and the ark back to the city, weeps on the Mount of Olives, prays that Ahithophel's counsel become foolishness, and sends Hushai the Archite back to Absalom to defeat that counsel and report through the priests' sons, as Absalom enters Jerusalem.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Absalom prepared a chariot, horses, and fifty runners, and at the gate won the hearts of Israelites by promising justice and kissing those who bowed to him. He got David's permission to go to Hebron under the pretext of a vow, sent spies to proclaim himself king there, and summoned Ahithophel. At the end of the unit he enters Jerusalem.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: David granted Absalom's request to go to Hebron, then on hearing that Israel's hearts followed Absalom, fled Jerusalem with his servants and household, leaving ten concubines to keep the house. He sent the ark back with Zadok, accepting whatever the LORD decides, wept barefoot with covered head on the Mount of Olives, prayed that Ahithophel's counsel be made foolish, and sent Hushai back as a spy.

l: Ahithophel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Ahithophel, David's counselor from Giloh, was sent for by Absalom while Absalom was offering sacrifices, and he joined the conspiracy. David was told of this and prayed that the LORD turn his counsel into foolishness.

l: Hushai the Archite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Hushai met David at the top of the Mount of Olives with torn tunic and earth on his head. David told him he would be a burden if he came along, and instead sent him to offer service to Absalom in order to defeat Ahithophel's counsel and report what he hears to Zadok and Abiathar. Hushai, called David's friend, entered the city.

l: Ittai the Gittite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: David urged Ittai, a foreigner and exile who had come only recently, to return and take his brothers back. Ittai swore by the LORD and the king's life to stay with David in death or life, and he passed over with all his men and little ones.

l: Zadok, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Zadok came with the Levites bearing the ark of the covenant, but David told him to carry it back into the city. David called him a seer, told him to return in peace with his son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar, and designated him with Abiathar as recipient of Hushai's reports.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: The men of Israel had their hearts stolen by Absalom's conduct at the gate. Spies were sent through all the tribes to proclaim Absalom king at the trumpet, and a messenger told David that Israel's hearts were after Absalom.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Jerusalem was the city David fled, fearing Absalom might strike it with the sword, leaving ten concubines to keep the house. The ark was returned there with Zadok and Abiathar, Hushai went in as David's friend, and Absalom entered it at the end of the unit.

l: Hebron, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: Hebron was the place Absalom claimed he would go to pay a vow to the LORD. It was actually where he arranged for spies to proclaim him king at the sound of the trumpet.

l: Absalom's conspiracy, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: The conspiracy grew through Absalom's gate-side courting of Israelites, spies sent through the tribes, and the unknowing participation of two hundred invited men from Jerusalem. It became strong when Ahithophel joined and the people increased continually with Absalom, prompting David's flight.

l: David's flight from Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 15
s: David ordered his servants to flee at once to avoid being overtaken and the city struck, and the king's household and people followed him out, crossing the Kidron toward the wilderness. Along the way Ittai pledged loyalty, the ark was sent back, and David went up the Mount of Olives weeping while arranging Hushai's return as an informant.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: As David flees past the top of the hill, Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth, brings him provisions and claims that Mephibosheth is staying in Jerusalem hoping to regain his father's kingdom; David then gives Ziba all that belonged to Mephibosheth. At Bahurim, Shimei son of Gera, of Saul's house, curses David and throws stones, and David stops Abishai from killing him, saying the LORD may have bidden him to curse. In Jerusalem, Hushai the Archite, David's friend, declares loyalty to Absalom, who questions him. Ahithophel advises Absalom to go in to his father's concubines in sight of all Israel, and Absalom does so on a tent atop the house. The text notes that Ahithophel's counsel was regarded as if inquired of God.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: David receives provisions from Ziba and gives him all that belonged to Mephibosheth. At Bahurim he endures Shimei's curses and stones, restrains Abishai, and says the LORD may repay him good for the cursing. He arrives weary with his people and refreshes himself.

l: Ziba, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth, meets David with saddled donkeys, bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine. He tells David that Mephibosheth is staying in Jerusalem expecting Israel to restore his father's kingdom, and David grants him all that belonged to Mephibosheth; Ziba bows and asks for favor.

l: Mephibosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Mephibosheth is reported by Ziba to be staying in Jerusalem, saying Israel will restore the kingdom of his father. On the strength of this report, David gives all that belonged to him to Ziba.

l: Shimei, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Shimei son of Gera, of Saul's house, comes out at Bahurim cursing David, throwing stones and dust, and calling him a man of blood who is paying for Saul's house and for losing the kingdom to Absalom. David forbids Abishai to kill him, and Shimei keeps cursing along the hillside.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Absalom comes to Jerusalem with the men of Israel and Ahithophel. He questions Hushai's loyalty, accepts his answer, asks Ahithophel for counsel, and follows it by going in to his father's concubines on a tent atop the house in sight of all Israel.

l: Ahithophel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Ahithophel is with Absalom in Jerusalem and advises him to go in to David's concubines so all Israel will hear he is abhorred by his father and his supporters will be strengthened. The text says his counsel was regarded as if inquired at the inner sanctuary of God, both with David and with Absalom.

l: Hushai the Archite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Hushai, David's friend, comes to Absalom and cries "Long live the king!" When Absalom asks why he did not go with his friend, Hushai answers that he will serve whomever the LORD, the people and Israel have chosen, and the son as he served the father.

l: concubines (David's ten concubines), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: David's concubines, whom he left to keep the house, are the object of Ahithophel's advice. Absalom goes in to them on a tent on the top of the house in the sight of all Israel.

l: Shimei’s cursing of David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Shimei curses David and throws stones and dust at him and his servants at Bahurim, calling him a man of blood. Abishai wants to behead Shimei, but David refuses, saying the LORD has invited the cursing and may repay him good for it.

l: Absalom's conspiracy, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 16
s: Absalom's rebellion advances as he and the men of Israel enter Jerusalem while David is away. He receives Hushai's pledge and Ahithophel's counsel, and publicly goes in to his father's concubines to show he is abhorred by his father.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Ahithophel advises Absalom to let him pursue David that night with twelve thousand men and strike only the king, but Absalom and the elders of Israel prefer the counsel of Hushai the Archite, who urges gathering all Israel and Absalom leading the battle in person. The LORD had ordained that Ahithophel's good counsel be defeated. Hushai tells Zadok and Abiathar to warn David, and Jonathan and Ahimaaz carry the message, hiding in a well at Bahurim with the help of a woman who misleads Absalom's servants. David and his people cross the Jordan before morning, and Ahithophel, seeing his counsel rejected, goes home and hangs himself. David reaches Mahanaim, Absalom crosses the Jordan and appoints Amasa over the army instead of Joab, and Shobi, Machir and Barzillai bring food and supplies to David's hungry people.

l: Ahithophel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Ahithophel advised Absalom to let him choose twelve thousand men and pursue David that night, striking only the king while he was weary. When his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, went home, set his house in order, hanged himself, and was buried in his father's tomb.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Absalom was pleased with Ahithophel's counsel but called Hushai the Archite to hear his view as well, and then he and the men of Israel judged Hushai's counsel better. He crossed the Jordan with all Israel, camped in Gilead, and set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. His servants searched for Jonathan and Ahimaaz after a boy told him of them but did not find them.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: David was warned through Hushai, the priests, Jonathan and Ahimaaz to pass over the water at once. He and all his people crossed the Jordan by morning, with none missing, and he came to Mahanaim, where Shobi, Machir and Barzillai supplied food and bedding for him and his people.

l: Hushai the Archite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Hushai told Absalom that Ahithophel's counsel was not good, describing David and his men as fierce mighty men and urging that all Israel be gathered and Absalom go to battle himself. His counsel was accepted, and he then told Zadok and Abiathar the priests to send word quickly to David not to lodge at the fords of the wilderness.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The elders of Israel were pleased with Ahithophel's saying, but Absalom and all the men of Israel then judged Hushai's counsel better. Israel crossed the Jordan with Absalom and encamped in the land of Gilead.

l: chosen men of Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The people with David were described as hungry, weary and thirsty in the wilderness. They crossed the Jordan with him by morning with none lacking, and were fed at Mahanaim with provisions brought by Shobi, Machir and Barzillai.

l: Jonathan, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Jonathan stayed with Ahimaaz by En Rogel, where a female servant reported to them, because they could not risk being seen entering the city. After a boy saw them and told Absalom, they fled to Bahurim and hid in a well, then came out and told King David to cross the water quickly.

l: Ahimaaz, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Ahimaaz stayed with Jonathan by En Rogel to carry word to King David. Seen by a boy, they hid in a well at Bahurim, escaped Absalom's servants, and then told David that Ahithophel had counseled against him and that he must cross the water quickly.

l: woman (of Bahurim), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The woman of the house in Bahurim spread a covering over the well's mouth and crushed grain on it so nothing was known. She told Absalom's servants that Jonathan and Ahimaaz had gone over the brook of water, so they gave up the search and returned to Jerusalem.

l: well (at Bahurim), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: The well in the court of a man's house in Bahurim served as the hiding place for Jonathan and Ahimaaz. It was covered and spread with crushed grain, and the two came up out of it after Absalom's servants left.

l: Jordan, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: David and all his people passed over the Jordan by morning light, with none left behind. Afterward Absalom and all the men of Israel also crossed it.

l: Ahithophel's counsel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Ahithophel's counsel was to pursue David that night with twelve thousand men, come on him weary, strike only the king, and bring the people back, which pleased Absalom and the elders. Nevertheless the LORD had ordained that this good counsel be defeated so that evil would come on Absalom, and it was not followed.

l: Hushai's counsel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: Hushai's counsel was to gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba and have Absalom lead the battle in person, falling on David like dew and dragging any city he entered into the river with ropes. Absalom and all the men of Israel judged it better than Ahithophel's counsel.

l: Ahithophel's suicide, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 17
s: When Ahithophel saw his counsel was not followed, he went to his city, set his house in order, and hanged himself. He died and was buried in the tomb of his father.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: David organizes his followers into captains and into three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, but the people persuade him to stay behind at the city gate, and he commands the captains to deal gently with Absalom. In the battle in the forest of Ephraim, Israel loses twenty thousand men, and the forest devours more than the sword. Absalom's head is caught in an oak and his mule runs on, and Joab, ignoring the king's command and the refusal of a man who saw it, thrusts three darts through Absalom's heart, and Joab's armor-bearers finish him. Joab calls off the pursuit, Absalom is cast into a pit under a heap of stones, and Ahimaaz and the Cushite race to bring news to David. When David learns Absalom is dead, he goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, wishing he had died instead.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: David counted his people, appointed captains, and divided them into three divisions, but yielded to the people's plea that he not go out to battle and instead stood beside the gate. He commanded Joab, Abishai, and Ittai to deal gently with Absalom, and later, on learning from the Cushite that Absalom was dead, he went up to the room over the gate and wept.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Absalom, riding his mule in the forest, was caught by his head in the boughs of a great oak and left hanging between sky and earth. Joab thrust three darts through his heart, ten of Joab's armor-bearers struck and killed him, and he was thrown into a great pit under a heap of stones. The text also notes that he had raised a pillar in the king's valley, since he had no son to keep his name, and it is still called Absalom's monument.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Joab led one third of the army and was told by a man that Absalom hung in an oak. He rebuked the man for not killing him, then himself thrust three darts into Absalom's heart despite the king's command. He then blew the trumpet to stop the pursuit, refused Ahimaaz the errand of bearing news that day, and sent the Cushite instead, though he finally let Ahimaaz run too.

l: Ahimaaz, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Ahimaaz son of Zadok asked to carry the king news that the LORD had avenged him, but Joab refused because the king's son was dead. He insisted on running anyway, outran the Cushite by way of the Plain, and the watchman recognized him by his running. He told David all was well and blessed the LORD, but when asked about Absalom said he saw a great tumult and did not know what it was.

l: Cushite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: The Cushite was told by Joab to go tell the king what he had seen, and he bowed to Joab and ran. He arrived after Ahimaaz, announced that the LORD had avenged the king, and when asked about Absalom answered that the king's enemies should be as that young man is, thereby revealing his death.

l: Israelite army (the people), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: David's people were set under captains and went out in three divisions, but they persuaded David not to go with them, saying he was worth ten thousand of them. They heard the king's command to deal gently with Absalom, fought in the forest of Ephraim, and returned from the pursuit when Joab blew the trumpet.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: Israel, the side opposing David, was struck down before David's servants in the forest of Ephraim, with twenty thousand men slain. After Joab stopped the pursuit and Absalom was buried under stones, all Israel fled, each man to his own tent.

l: forest of Ephraim, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: The forest of Ephraim was the site of the battle between David's servants and Israel. The battle spread over the whole countryside, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword did. Absalom was cast into a great pit in the forest and covered with stones.

l: oak (in the forest of Ephraim), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: A great oak with thick boughs caught Absalom's head as his mule passed beneath, leaving him hanging between sky and earth. Joab thrust three darts through Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the oak.

l: battle in the forest of Ephraim, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: David's forces, in three divisions under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, fought Israel in the forest of Ephraim, and twenty thousand of Israel were slain. The battle spread across the country, and the forest claimed more lives than the sword. It ended when Joab blew the trumpet after Absalom's death, and the people returned from the pursuit.

l: David's mourning for Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 18
s: After hearing from the Cushite that Absalom was dead, David was much moved and went up to the room over the gate and wept. He cried out, "My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! I wish I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son!"

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Joab learns that King David is weeping for Absalom, and the people's victory turns to mourning; Joab rebukes David for shaming those who saved him and warns that everyone will desert him unless he comforts them. David sits in the gate, then sends Zadok and Abiathar to urge the elders of Judah to bring him back, and offers Amasa the captaincy of the army in place of Joab. David crosses the Jordan, where he pardons Shimei over Abishai's objection, hears Mephibosheth's explanation for not following him and tells him to divide the land with Ziba, and blesses Barzillai, who declines to come to Jerusalem and sends Chimham instead. The chapter ends with the men of Israel and the men of Judah quarreling over who has the greater claim to the king, with Judah's words proving fiercer.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: David covers his face and cries out for Absalom until Joab rebukes him, after which he sits in the gate and sends word to the elders of Judah to bring him back. He offers Amasa the captaincy in place of Joab, swears to spare Shimei, tells Mephibosheth and Ziba to divide the land, and takes Chimham with him after kissing and blessing Barzillai.

l: Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Absalom is mourned by David, who cries out "My son Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son!" The people also note that he, whom they had anointed over them, is dead in battle, and Joab says David would have been pleased if Absalom had lived and everyone else had died.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Joab is told of the king's weeping and confronts David, saying he has shamed his servants who saved his life and swearing that no man will stay with him that night unless he goes out to comfort them. David then declares he will make Amasa captain of the army instead of Joab.

l: Shimei, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Shimei, son of Gera the Benjamite of Bahurim, hurries to meet David at the Jordan with a thousand men of Benjamin and confesses that he sinned. Abishai wants him put to death for cursing the LORD's anointed, but David swears that he will not die.

l: Mephibosheth, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Mephibosheth comes to meet David, having not groomed his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes since the king left. He says his servant deceived him and slandered him, and David tells him and Ziba to divide the land; Mephibosheth replies that Ziba may take all, since the king has returned in peace.

l: Barzillai the Gileadite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Barzillai, an eighty-year-old great man from Rogelim who had provided for David at Mahanaim, escorts the king over the Jordan. He declines David's offer to sustain him in Jerusalem because of his age, asks to die in his own city, and offers Chimham instead; David agrees, kisses and blesses him, and he returns home.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: The men of Judah are moved as one man to send for David to return, and they come to Gilgal to bring him over the Jordan. When Israel complains, they answer that the king is their close relative and that they have received no gifts at his cost, and their words prove fiercer than Israel's.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: Israel's people, who had fled each to his tent, argue among themselves about bringing the king back, and then half of them help bring him over. The men of Israel accuse Judah of stealing the king away, claim ten parts in him and more claim to David, and complain that their advice was not sought first.

l: the people, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: The people hear that the king grieves for his son, and their victory turns to mourning as they sneak into the city like those ashamed after fleeing a battle. After David sits in the gate they all come before him, and later all the people cross the Jordan with him.

l: David's mourning for Absalom, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: David's loud weeping with covered face over Absalom turns the day's victory into mourning for the people. Joab's rebuke ends it, as David arises and sits in the gate.

l: David's return to Jerusalem, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: David prompts the return by sending Zadok and Abiathar to the elders of Judah, and Judah sends word for him and his servants to return. He comes to the Jordan, where Judah meets him at Gilgal, and he crosses and proceeds to Gilgal, with the account in this unit ending before he reaches Jerusalem.

l: dispute between Israel and Judah over the king, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 19
s: The men of Israel protest that Judah stole the king away and brought him over the Jordan with his household and men. Judah answers that the king is a close relative and that they gained nothing at his cost, while Israel claims ten parts in him; the quarrel remains unresolved, with Judah's words fiercer.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite, blows a trumpet and rallies the men of Israel away from David, while Judah stays loyal. David returns to Jerusalem, shuts up his ten concubines, and orders Amasa to gather Judah's men; when Amasa is late, David sends Abishai and Joab's men after Sheba. Joab kills Amasa with a sword at Gibeon, and the people follow Joab in pursuit of Sheba. At Abel of Beth Maacah, Joab besieges the city until a wise woman negotiates with him, and the city's people cut off Sheba's head and throw it over the wall. Joab blows the trumpet, the army disperses, and Joab returns to Jerusalem; the chapter ends with a list of David's officials.

l: Sheba the son of Bichri, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Sheba, a wicked Benjamite, blows a trumpet and calls Israel to abandon David, and the men of Israel follow him. David fears he will do more harm than Absalom did. Pursued to Abel of Beth Maacah, he is beheaded by the city's people, and his head is thrown to Joab.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: David returns to Jerusalem and puts his ten concubines in custody, providing for them but not going in to them, so they live as widows until death. He tells Amasa to gather Judah's men within three days, and when Amasa delays he sends Abishai to pursue Sheba. Joab ultimately ends the revolt and returns to him, and a list of his officials follows.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Joab, with Abishai his brother, leads the pursuit of Sheba. He greets Amasa as a brother, takes him by the beard, and kills him with a sword, after which the people follow him. He besieges Abel of Beth Maacah, accepts the wise woman's offer to deliver Sheba's head, blows the trumpet to end the siege, and returns to Jerusalem; he is named over all the army of Israel.

l: Amasa, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Amasa is told by David to gather the men of Judah within three days but stays longer than the appointed time. He meets Joab at the great stone in Gibeon and, not heeding the sword in Joab's hand, is struck in the body and dies. His body is moved from the highway into a field and covered with a garment.

l: wise woman (of Abel of Beth Maacah), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: The wise woman calls from the city to Joab and argues that Abel is a peaceable, faithful city and a mother in Israel that should not be destroyed. After Joab says he wants only Sheba, she promises his head will be thrown over the wall. She persuades the people in her wisdom, and they behead Sheba.

l: Abel of Beth Maacah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: Abel of Beth Maacah is where Sheba takes refuge and where Joab's forces besiege it, building a mound and battering the wall. The woman describes it as a place once known for giving counsel. The siege ends when its people kill Sheba and throw his head to Joab.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 20
s: The men of Israel leave David to follow Sheba, while Judah stays with the king from the Jordan to Jerusalem. After Sheba's death, the people disperse, each man to his tent. The chapter closes by listing David's officials over the army, the Cherethites and Pelethites, forced labor, records, and priests.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: A three-year famine leads David to seek the LORD, who says it is because Saul put the Gibeonites to death. David asks the Gibeonites what atonement they want, and they ask for seven of Saul's sons to be hanged; David spares Mephibosheth son of Jonathan because of his oath, and hands over Rizpah's two sons and Merab's five sons. Rizpah guards the bodies from birds and animals until rain falls, and David, hearing of it, retrieves the bones of Saul and Jonathan and buries them with the bones of those hanged in Kish's tomb, after which God answers prayer for the land. The chapter then records renewed wars with the Philistines, in which David grows faint and is rescued by Abishai, and four descendants of the giant are killed by David and his servants.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: David seeks the LORD during the famine, learns it is because of Saul's killing of the Gibeonites, and agrees to give them whatever they ask. He spares Mephibosheth son of Jonathan because of their oath, hands seven of Saul's descendants to the Gibeonites, and later gathers the bones of Saul, Jonathan and those hanged for burial. In the Philistine wars he grows faint and is saved by Abishai, and his men swear he must no longer go to battle lest he quench the lamp of Israel.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: The LORD answers David's seeking by declaring the famine is for Saul and his bloody house because he put the Gibeonites to death. The Gibeonites hang the men before the LORD, and after the bones are buried, God answers prayer for the land.

l: Saul, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Saul is blamed for the famine because he put the Gibeonites to death in his zeal for Israel and Judah, though Israel had sworn to them. Seven of his descendants are hanged in atonement, and his bones, along with Jonathan's, are recovered from the men of Jabesh Gilead and buried in Zela in the tomb of his father Kish.

l: Gibeonites, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: The Gibeonites are described as a remnant of the Amorites to whom Israel had sworn an oath, whom Saul sought to kill. They refuse silver or gold, ask that seven of Saul's sons be delivered to them, and hang them on the mountain before the LORD in Gibeah of Saul.

l: famine, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: A famine lasts three years, year after year, in David's days. The LORD attributes it to Saul's killing of the Gibeonites, and after the atonement and burials, God answers prayer for the land.

l: Rizpah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Rizpah, daughter of Aiah and concubine of Saul, is the mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth, two of the men handed over and hanged. She spreads sackcloth on the rock and from the start of harvest until rain falls keeps birds by day and animals by night from the bodies, and her deed is reported to David.

l: seven sons of Saul's house, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Seven men are delivered to the Gibeonites: Armoni and Mephibosheth, sons of Rizpah and Saul, and the five sons of Merab daughter of Saul, borne to Adriel. They are hanged on the mountain before the LORD at the start of barley harvest, all falling together, and their bones are later gathered and buried with those of Saul and Jonathan.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: The Philistines had earlier hanged the bodies of Saul and Jonathan at Beth Shan, and they war again with Israel. Their giants, descended from the giant of Gath, are killed at Gob and Gath by David and his servants.

l: Ishbibenob, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Ishbibenob, one of the sons of the giant, carries a bronze spear weighing three hundred shekels and a new sword. He thinks he will kill the faint David but is struck down and killed by Abishai.

l: Abishai, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 21
s: Abishai, son of Zeruiah, helps David when he grows faint in battle and strikes and kills the Philistine Ishbibenob. After this David's men swear that David will no longer go out with them to battle.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: Chapter 22 presents a song David spoke to the LORD on the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from Saul. David praises the LORD as his rock, fortress, shield and savior, and recounts calling on him in distress amid the cords of Sheol and snares of death. He describes the LORD's stormy descent, with quaking earth, fire, thunder, darkness and lightning, to draw him out of many waters. David claims the LORD rewarded his righteousness and clean hands, and credits the LORD with arming him for battle so that he destroyed his enemies, who cried out without being answered. The song ends with David vowing to give thanks among the nations and praising the LORD for deliverance to his king, David, and his offspring forever.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: David speaks this song to the LORD after being delivered from all his enemies and from Saul. He recounts distress, rescue, and his own righteousness, and says the LORD trained him for war, made him head of the nations, and enabled him to destroy his enemies. He vows to give thanks among the nations and is named as the LORD's anointed, to whom loving kindness is shown forever along with his offspring.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: The LORD is praised as David's rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, high tower and savior, who hears his cry from his temple. He comes down in storm and fire to rescue David, rewards righteousness, saves the afflicted, brings down the arrogant, and arms David for battle. He is exalted as the God who executes vengeance, lives, and gives great deliverance to his king.

l: enemies (David's enemies), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: David's enemies, including the strong enemy who hated him and Saul, come against him in his calamity but are too mighty only in comparison to David alone. With the LORD's help David pursues, strikes down and crushes them, and they cannot rise. When they look for someone to save them and cry to the LORD, he does not answer, and foreigners come trembling and submit to David.

l: the LORD's theophany (storm and deliverance of David), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: In response to David's cry, the LORD appears in a storm: the earth shakes, smoke and consuming fire come from his mouth, he rides a cherub on the wind, and he thunders from heaven. His arrows and lightning scatter enemies, the sea's channels and the world's foundations are laid bare at his rebuke, and he draws David out of many waters.

l: David's song of deliverance, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 22
s: The song is spoken to the LORD on the day he delivered David from his enemies and Saul. It moves from praise and a report of distress, through the storm theophany and David's claim of righteousness, to victory over enemies and rule over nations. It closes with thanksgiving among the nations and a declaration of the LORD's lasting kindness to David and his offspring.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Chapter 23 opens with David's last words, in which he says the LORD's Spirit spoke through him and describes a righteous ruler as morning light, while the ungodly are like thorns burned with fire. It then lists the mighty men of David, beginning with Josheb Basshebeth, Eleazar, and Shammah the son of Agee, who won victories against the Philistines with the LORD's help. Three of the thirty broke through the Philistine camp to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, and David poured it out to the LORD instead of drinking it. Abishai and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada are praised for their deeds but are not counted among the three. The chapter ends with a list of the thirty, closing with Uriah the Hittite, thirty-seven in all.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David speaks his last words, calling himself the anointed of the God of Jacob and the sweet psalmist of Israel, and affirms that God made an everlasting covenant with his house. He longs for water from the well of Bethlehem while the Philistines hold the town, and when three mighty men bring it, he refuses to drink it and pours it out to the LORD. He sets Benaiah over his guard.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The LORD's Spirit is said to have spoken by David, and the LORD is called the God and Rock of Israel who made an everlasting covenant with David's house. He works great victories through Eleazar and Shammah the son of Agee. David pours the water out to the LORD as an offering.

l: Eleazar, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Eleazar the son of Dodai the son of an Ahohite is one of the three mighty men with David. He stood and struck the Philistines until his hand was weary and froze to his sword, after the men of Israel had gone away. The LORD worked a great victory, and the people returned only to take plunder.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The Philistines gather to battle and are defied and struck down by Eleazar, and Shammah the son of Agee kills them in the lentil field. Their troop is encamped in the valley of Rephaim and their garrison holds Bethlehem. Three mighty men break through their army to reach the well of Bethlehem.

l: Shammah the son of Agee, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Shammah the son of Agee, a Hararite, is named as a mighty man. When the people fled from the Philistines gathered at a plot full of lentils, he stood in the middle of the plot, defended it, and killed the Philistines. The LORD worked a great victory.

l: three mighty men, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Three of the thirty chief men came to David at the cave of Adullam at harvest time. They broke through the Philistine army, drew water from the well of Bethlehem by the gate, and brought it to David, who poured it out to the LORD. Eleazar is named among the three, and Abishai was their chief but was not counted as one of them. Benaiah was more honorable than the thirty but did not attain to the three.

l: mighty men of David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The mighty men are listed by name, led by Josheb Basshebeth, chief of the captains, who killed eight hundred at one time. They include the three, Abishai, Benaiah, and the thirty, ending with Uriah the Hittite and a total of thirty-seven. Their deeds include victories over the Philistines, an Egyptian, and a lion.

l: Bethlehem, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Bethlehem is held by a Philistine garrison while David is in the stronghold. David longs for water from its well by the gate. Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem is listed among the thirty.

l: well of Bethlehem, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: The well of Bethlehem is by the gate, and David longs to drink from it. Three mighty men break through the Philistine army to draw water from it and bring it to him.

l: Abishai, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Abishai, brother of Joab and son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three. He lifted his spear against three hundred and killed them, and gained a name among the three. He was made their captain as the most honorable of them, but he was not included as one of the three.

l: Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: Benaiah, son of Jehoiada and of a valiant man of Kabzeel, killed the two sons of Ariel of Moab and a lion in a pit in a time of snow. He killed a huge Egyptian by taking the spear from his hand with a staff and using it against him. He was more honorable than the thirty but did not attain to the three, and David set him over his guard.

l: David's last words, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: David's last words say the LORD's Spirit spoke by him and that a righteous ruler who fears God is like the morning light after rain. He says God made an everlasting covenant with his house, ordered and sure. The ungodly will be like thorns, burned utterly with fire.

l: water offering, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 23
s: When the three mighty men bring David the water from the well of Bethlehem, he will not drink it and pours it out to the LORD. He says it is the blood of men who risked their lives to go.

l: The Second Book of Samuel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The LORD, angry with Israel, moves David to order a census, and David commands Joab and the army captains to count the people from Dan to Beersheba despite Joab's objection. After nine months and twenty days Joab reports 800,000 swordsmen in Israel and 500,000 in Judah, and David's heart strikes him, so he confesses his sin. Through the prophet Gad the LORD offers David a choice of seven years of famine, three months of flight from foes, or three days of pestilence, and David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand. The pestilence kills seventy thousand before the LORD's angel, at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite, is told to stop. At Gad's direction David buys the threshing floor from Araunah for fifty shekels of silver, builds an altar, and offers sacrifices, and the plague is removed from Israel.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The LORD, angry with Israel, moves David to order the census, then sends Gad to offer David a choice of three punishments. He sends a pestilence that kills seventy thousand, relents when the angel stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem, and is entreated for the land after David's sacrifices, removing the plague.

l: David, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: David, moved by the LORD, orders Joab to count the people and overrides Joab's objection. Afterward his heart strikes him, he confesses that he has sinned greatly, chooses to fall into the LORD's hand, and pleads that the LORD's hand be against him and his father's house instead of the people. He buys Araunah's threshing floor at full price, saying he will not offer burnt offerings that cost him nothing, builds an altar, and offers burnt and peace offerings.

l: Joab, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: Joab, captain of the army, objects to the census, asking why the king delights in this thing, but the king's word prevails over him and the captains. He leads the count across the land in nine months and twenty days and reports 800,000 valiant men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah.

l: Gad, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: Gad, David's seer and a prophet, receives the LORD's word and brings David the offer of three punishments, asking for an answer to return. Later he tells David to go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

l: Araunah the Jebusite, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: Araunah sees the king coming and bows to him with his face to the ground. He offers the threshing floor, cattle, sledges and yokes freely to David, but David insists on paying, and Araunah sells them for fifty shekels of silver.

l: angel (the LORD’s angel), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The angel who destroys the people stretches out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it. The LORD tells him it is enough and to withdraw his hand, and he is by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: Israel is the object of the LORD's anger and is counted from Dan to Beersheba, with 800,000 swordsmen reported, besides 500,000 in Judah. Seventy thousand of its people die in the pestilence, which is removed from Israel after David's offerings.

l: census of Israel and Judah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The census is ordered by David at the LORD's prompting, over Joab's objection. It covers the land from across the Jordan to Dan, Sidon, Tyre and Beersheba, takes nine months and twenty days, and yields 800,000 in Israel and 500,000 in Judah. David afterward calls it a sin and a foolish act.

l: pestilence, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The pestilence is one of three options the LORD offers, and David chooses it. It falls on Israel from morning until the appointed time and kills seventy thousand from Dan to Beersheba. It is halted before Jerusalem is destroyed and removed after David's sacrifices.

l: threshing floor of Araunah, The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: The threshing floor is where the LORD's angel stands when the LORD stops the destruction. Gad directs David to build an altar there, and David buys it with the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.

l: altar (David’s altar to the LORD), The Second Book of Samuel, Chapter 24
s: David builds the altar on Araunah's threshing floor at Gad's direction after paying for the site. He offers burnt offerings and peace offerings on it, and the LORD is entreated for the land and the plague is removed from Israel.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Proverbs chapter 1 opens by naming the proverbs of Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, and stating their purpose: to give wisdom, instruction, prudence and understanding to the simple and the young, and to increase the learning of the wise. It declares that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge while fools despise wisdom and instruction. A father urges his son to heed parental teaching and refuse sinners who entice him to join in ambush, bloodshed and plunder, warning that such greed destroys those who pursue it. Wisdom then calls aloud in the streets and city gates, rebuking the simple, mockers and fools for refusing her counsel, and warns that disaster will come and she will not answer them. She promises that whoever listens to her will dwell securely and without fear of harm.

l: Solomon, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Solomon, the son of David and king of Israel, is named as the source of the proverbs that open the book. The text presents the proverbs as given to impart wisdom, instruction, righteousness, justice and equity.

l: LORD, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: The LORD is named in the statement that fear of him is the beginning of knowledge. Wisdom later says that those who face disaster did not choose the fear of the LORD.

l: Wisdom, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Wisdom is personified as a woman who calls aloud in the streets, public squares, noisy places and city gates. She rebukes the simple, mockers and fools for refusing her, says she will laugh at their disaster and not answer when they call, and promises that whoever listens to her will dwell securely without fear of harm.

l: son (the addressee), Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: The son is told to listen to his father's instruction and not forsake his mother's teaching, which will be a garland and chains for him. He is warned not to consent to sinners who entice him and not to walk on their path.

l: sinners (those who entice the son), Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Sinners invite the son to lie in wait for the innocent, shed blood, seize wealth and share one purse with them. The text says their feet run to evil and that they in fact lie in wait for their own blood and lives.

l: the simple, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: The simple ones are asked by Wisdom how long they will love simplicity. The text says their backsliding will kill them, while the proverbs aim to give prudence to the simple.

l: fools, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Fools despise wisdom and instruction and hate knowledge. Wisdom says their careless ease will destroy them and that they will eat the fruit of their own way and be filled with their own schemes.

l: wisdom, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Wisdom and instruction are the goal of the proverbs, which are meant to help people know and receive them. The foolish despise them, while the father's and mother's teaching is likened to a garland and chains of grace.

l: greed and violent plunder, Proverbs, Proverbs / Chapter 1
s: Greed and violent plunder appear in the sinners' scheme to ambush the innocent and fill their houses with loot. The text says such ways take away the life of those who are greedy for gain, as the plunderers ambush their own lives.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 is addressed to 'my son' and sets out a conditional path to wisdom: if he receives the speaker's words, seeks understanding like silver and hidden treasure, then he will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God. The LORD is the giver of wisdom, knowledge and understanding, and acts as a shield and guard for the upright who walk in integrity. Wisdom and discretion will protect the son by delivering him from evil men who forsake uprightness and delight in perverseness, and from the strange woman, a foreigner who flatters, forsakes the friend of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God. Her house leads to death and none who go to her return. The chapter closes by urging the son to walk with good men, since the upright will dwell in the land while the wicked and treacherous will be cut off and rooted out.

l: LORD, Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: The LORD gives wisdom, and knowledge and understanding come out of his mouth.
