He lays up sound wisdom for the upright, acts as a shield to those who walk in integrity, and guards the paths of justice and preserves the way of his saints. Knowing him is the result of seeking wisdom: the son will understand the fear of the LORD and find the knowledge of God.

l: wisdom, Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: Wisdom is to be sought like silver and hidden treasure, and the LORD is its giver. When it enters the son's heart, knowledge becomes pleasant to his soul, and wisdom with discretion and understanding watches over and keeps him, delivering him from evil.

l: understanding, Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: Understanding is something the son is to call out for and lift his voice for, and the LORD's mouth is its source. It will keep the son and deliver him from the way of evil and from the strange woman, and it brings knowledge of righteousness, justice, equity and every good path.

l: son (the addressee), Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: The son is urged to receive the speaker's words, store up his commandments, turn his ear to wisdom and apply his heart to understanding. If he seeks her earnestly, he will understand the fear of the LORD and be delivered from evil men and the strange woman. He is told to walk in the way of good men and keep the paths of the righteous.

l: the righteous, Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: The upright are those for whom the LORD lays up sound wisdom, and those who walk in integrity have him as a shield. The text says the upright will dwell in the land and the perfect will remain in it.

l: the wicked, Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: Evil men speak perverse things, forsake the paths of uprightness to walk in darkness, rejoice to do evil, and are crooked and wayward in their paths. The son is to be delivered from them, and the wicked and treacherous are said to be cut off and rooted out of the land.

l: strange woman (the seductress), Proverbs, Chapter 2
s: The strange woman, also called the foreigner, flatters with her words, forsakes the friend of her youth, and forgets the covenant of her God. Her house leads down to death and her paths to the departed spirits, and none who go to her return or attain the paths of life. The son is to be delivered from her.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, a father figure addresses his son, urging him to hold onto his teaching, kindness, and truth, and promising long life, peace, and favor in return. The son is told to trust the LORD fully rather than his own understanding, to honor the LORD with his substance, and to accept the LORD's discipline as a father's correction. The chapter praises wisdom as more valuable than silver, gold, or rubies, a tree of life that brings long days, riches, honor, and peace, and credits it with the LORD's founding of the earth. The son is then told to keep wisdom so he may walk securely and sleep without fear, and to do good to his neighbor, avoid needless strife, and not envy violent men. It closes by contrasting how the LORD treats the perverse, wicked, and mockers with how he treats the upright, righteous, and humble, and the wise inherit glory while fools receive shame.

l: LORD, Proverbs, Chapter 3
s: The LORD is to be trusted with all one's heart and honored with the first fruits of one's increase, and he disciplines those he loves as a father corrects a son he delights in. By wisdom he founded the earth, by understanding he established the heavens, and by his knowledge the depths were broken up and the skies drop dew. He will be the son's confidence and keep his foot from being taken; he finds the perverse an abomination, befriends the upright, curses the house of the wicked, blesses the habitation of the righteous, mocks the mockers, and gives grace to the humble.

l: Wisdom, Proverbs, Chapter 3
s: Wisdom is described as bringing happiness to whoever finds her, with profit and return better than silver and fine gold and a worth beyond rubies. In her right hand is length of days and in her left riches and honor, her ways are pleasant and her paths peace, and she is a tree of life to those who hold her. The LORD used wisdom to found the earth, and the wise will inherit glory.

l: son (the addressee), Proverbs, Chapter 3
s: The son is urged to keep his father's teaching and commandments, to bind kindness and truth around his neck, to trust the LORD rather than his own understanding, and to honor the LORD with his substance. He is told not to despise the LORD's discipline, to keep sound wisdom and discretion so he can walk securely and sleep sweetly, to do good to his neighbor without delay, and to avoid causeless strife and envy of violent men. In return he is promised long life, peace, favor, health, plenty, and a life free of fear.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4, a father urges his sons to heed his instruction and not forsake his law, recalling that his own father taught him to get wisdom and understanding at any cost. He promises that wisdom, if loved and embraced, will preserve, exalt, and honor them, and that instruction will lengthen their lives and keep their steps unhindered. He warns them away from the path of the wicked, who cannot sleep unless they do evil and who live on wickedness and violence. He contrasts this with the path of the righteous, which is like growing dawn light, while the way of the wicked is darkness in which they stumble unknowingly. He closes by telling his son to guard his heart, keep his mouth and lips free of corruption, look straight ahead, and turn neither right nor left but away from evil.

l: father (the speaker), Proverbs, Chapter 4
s: The father urges his sons to listen to his instruction and not forsake his law, recalling that he was once a tender only child taught by his own father. He says he has taught them in the way of wisdom and led them in straight paths. He commands them to keep their hearts, avoid the path of the wicked, and turn away from evil.

l: sons (the addressees), Proverbs, Chapter 4
s: The sons are told to listen, receive the father's sayings, get wisdom and understanding, and hold firmly to instruction. They are warned not to enter the path of the wicked and are told to guard their hearts, put away a perverse mouth, look straight ahead, and not turn to the right or left. If they obey, the years of their life will be many and their steps will not be hampered.

l: wisdom, Proverbs, Chapter 4
s: Wisdom is called supreme and is to be obtained even at the cost of all one's possessions. If she is not forsaken, loved, esteemed, and embraced, she will preserve and keep a person, exalt and honor him, and give him a garland of grace and a crown of splendor. Instruction, spoken of as her, is described as life itself.

l: the wicked, Proverbs, Chapter 4
s: The wicked do not sleep unless they do evil, and their sleep is taken away unless they make someone fall. They eat the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of violence. Their way is like darkness, and they do not know what they stumble over.

l: the righteous, Proverbs, Chapter 4
s: The path of the righteous is compared to the dawning light that shines more and more until the perfect day. This stands in contrast to the darkness of the wicked.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: In Chapter 5, a father addresses his son (and sons), urging him to heed his wisdom and keep discretion. He warns that an adulteress's speech is smooth as honey and oil but ends bitter and deadly, leading to death and Sheol, and he tells the son to stay far from her house lest he lose his honor, years, and wealth to strangers. He pictures the son groaning in the end, lamenting that he despised instruction and ignored his teachers. He then urges faithfulness, comparing marital love to drinking from one's own cistern and well, and telling the son to rejoice in the wife of his youth and be captivated by her love. He closes by stating that the LORD sees all human paths, and that the wicked are ensnared by their own sin and die for lack of instruction.

l: strange woman (the seductress), Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: The adulteress is described as having lips that drip honey and a mouth smoother than oil, yet in the end she is as bitter as wormwood and as sharp as a two-edged sword. Her feet go down to death and her steps lead to Sheol; she gives no thought to the way of life, and her ways are crooked without her knowing it. The son is warned not to come near her house or be captivated by her.

l: son (the speaker's son), Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: The son is told to pay attention to the speaker's wisdom, keep away from the adulteress, and not come near the door of her house. He is warned that otherwise he will lose his honor, years, and wealth, and will groan at the end, regretting that he despised instruction. He is urged to drink from his own cistern, rejoice in the wife of his youth, and be captivated always by her love.

l: speaker (the father/teacher), Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: The speaker calls on his son, and then his sons, to listen to his wisdom and understanding and not depart from the words of his mouth. He warns against the adulteress, describes the regret that follows ignoring instruction, and commends faithful love to his wife. He frames his teaching as the instruction whose lack leads to death.

l: LORD, Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: The LORD is said to have the ways of man before his eyes and to examine all his paths. This is given as the reason the wicked are ensnared by their own evil deeds and held by the cords of their sin.

l: wife of your youth, Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: The wife of the son's youth is presented as the rightful source of his satisfaction, likened to his own spring, a loving doe, and a graceful deer. The son is told to rejoice in her, let her breasts satisfy him at all times, and be captivated always with her love.

l: instruction, Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: Instruction is something the son is urged to heed, and its rejection is the source of the regret he is pictured voicing at his end: he hated instruction, despised reproof, and did not obey his teachers. The chapter closes by saying the wicked man will die for lack of instruction and go astray in the greatness of his folly.

l: adultery and fidelity, Proverbs, Chapter 5
s: Adultery is portrayed as ending in death, loss of honor, years, and wealth to strangers, and ruin. Fidelity is portrayed through the images of drinking water from one's own cistern and well, keeping one's springs for oneself alone, and rejoicing in the wife of one's youth. The chapter asks why the son should be captivated by an adulteress or embrace another's bosom.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 gives a father's warnings to his son on four dangers. The son is told to free himself at once if he has pledged collateral for a neighbor or stranger, and to learn diligence from the ant, in contrast to the sluggard whose sleep brings poverty. It describes the worthless person with a perverse mouth who sows discord and faces sudden calamity, and lists six things, indeed seven, that the LORD hates. It closes by urging the son to keep his father's commandment and his mother's teaching so they guard him from the immoral woman, and warns that adultery with a neighbor's wife brings burning, disgrace, and a husband's unrelenting vengeance.

l: ant, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The ant is held up as a model of wisdom. Having no chief, overseer, or ruler, she provides her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest.

l: sluggard, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The sluggard is told to consider the ant and is asked how long he will sleep. His little sleep and folding of the hands will bring poverty on him like a robber and scarcity like an armed man.

l: LORD, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The LORD is said to hate six things, indeed seven that are an abomination to him. These are listed as arrogant eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a scheming heart, feet swift to mischief, a lying false witness, and one who sows discord among brothers.

l: worthless person, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The worthless person, a man of iniquity, walks with a perverse mouth, winks, signals with his feet, and motions with his fingers. His heart devises evil and sows discord, so his calamity will come suddenly and he will be broken without remedy.

l: prostitute and wayward wife, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The immoral woman is described with a flattering, wayward tongue and captivating eyelids. The son is warned not to lust after her beauty, since a prostitute reduces a man to a piece of bread and the adulteress hunts for his precious life.

l: neighbor's wife, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The neighbor's wife is the woman with whom going in brings the same harm as scooping fire into one's lap. Whoever touches her will not go unpunished.

l: adulterer, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The adulterer is called void of understanding and is said to destroy his own soul. He gets wounds and lasting dishonor, and the wronged husband, furious with jealousy, will spare no vengeance and accept no ransom or gifts.

l: collateral and pledge, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: Becoming collateral or striking hands in pledge for a neighbor or stranger is described as a trap, ensnaring the son by the words of his mouth. He is urged to act immediately, giving no sleep to his eyes, to escape it.

l: things the LORD hates, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: Six things, and a seventh, are named as abominations to the LORD: arrogant eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising wicked schemes, feet swift to mischief, a false witness who utters lies, and one who sows discord among brothers.

l: commandment and teaching, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: The son is told to keep his father's commandment and not forsake his mother's teaching, binding them on his heart and neck. They lead him when he walks, watch over him when he sleeps, and talk with him when he wakes. The commandment is called a lamp, the law light, and reproofs the way of life, keeping him from the immoral woman.

l: adultery, Proverbs, Chapter 6
s: Adultery is compared to scooping fire into one's lap or walking on hot coals, which cannot be done without burns. Unlike a hungry thief who is not despised, the adulterer faces destruction of his soul, unwiped reproach, and a husband's vengeance.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 7
s: In Chapter 7, a father addresses his son and urges him to keep his words and commandments, to treat them as precious, and to call wisdom his sister so that she will protect him from the strange woman. The speaker then describes watching from his lattice window as a young man void of understanding walks toward the strange woman's house at twilight. She meets him dressed as a prostitute, kisses him, and persuades him with talk of her peace offerings, her perfumed bed, and her husband being away on a long journey until the full moon. The young man follows her at once, like an ox to slaughter, and the speaker warns his sons not to let their hearts turn to her ways, since her house is the way to Sheol and the rooms of death.

l: speaker (the father/teacher), Proverbs, Chapter 7
s: The speaker addresses his son, urging him to keep his words and commandments and to call wisdom his sister. He recounts watching from his lattice window as a young man was seduced, then turns to his sons with a warning to avoid the strange woman's paths because her house leads to death.

l: strange woman (the seductress), Proverbs, Chapter 7
s: The strange woman meets the young man in the street dressed as a prostitute and with crafty intent. She is described as loud, defiant, and always lurking in streets and squares. She kisses him and, claiming to have paid her vows, invites him to her perfumed bed because her husband has gone on a long journey and will return at the full moon. Her flattering words lead him astray, and the speaker says she has thrown down many wounded and that all her slain are a mighty army.

l: young man (void of understanding), Proverbs, Chapter 7
s: The young man is seen among the simple ones, passing near the strange woman's corner and heading toward her house in the twilight. She catches and seduces him, and he follows her immediately like an ox going to slaughter or a bird hurrying to a snare, not knowing it will cost his life.

l: wisdom and understanding, Proverbs, Chapter 7
s: The speaker tells his son to say to wisdom, "You are my sister," and to call understanding his relative. This kinship is meant to keep him from the strange woman and her flattering words.

l: commandments and teaching (the speaker's), Proverbs, Chapter 7
s: The speaker tells his son to keep his words and commandments, to lay them up within him, and to guard his teaching as the apple of his eye. He is to bind them on his fingers and write them on the tablet of his heart, and the text says that keeping the commandments brings life.

l: Proverbs, Proverbs, Chapter 8
s: In Chapter 8, wisdom is personified as a woman who calls out at high places, city gates, and crossroads to the simple, the fools, and all the sons of mankind. She says her words are true, righteous, and better than silver, gold, or rubies, and that she hates evil, pride, and arrogance. She claims that kings and princes rule by her, that she loves those who love her, and that she gives riches, honor, and enduring wealth. She describes herself as possessed by the LORD at the beginning, born before the depths, mountains, and earth, and present as a craftsman and delight by his side when he established the heavens, the sea's boundary, and the earth's foundations. She closes by urging her sons to listen and watch at her gates, saying that whoever finds her finds life and favor from the LORD, while those who sin against her wrong their souls and those who hate her love death.

l: strange woman (the seductress), Proverbs, Chapter 8
s: Wisdom cries out in public places, at high places, crossroads, and city gates, calling the simple and fools to understanding. She declares her words true and righteous, says she hates evil, pride, and arrogance, and claims counsel, power, riches, and honor, with kings and rulers reigning by her. She says the LORD possessed her before creation, that she was present as a craftsman and a delight by his side, and that she delighted in the sons of men; whoever finds her finds life, and those who hate her love death.

l: LORD, Proverbs, Chapter 8
s: The LORD possessed wisdom in the beginning of his work, before his deeds of old. He established the heavens, set a circle on the surface of the deep, established the clouds, strengthened the springs of the deep, gave the sea its boundary, and marked out the earth's foundations. Fear of him is said to be hating evil, and whoever finds wisdom obtains favor from him.

l: men (sons of mankind), Proverbs, Chapter 8
s: The sons of mankind, including the simple and fools, are addressed by wisdom's voice and urged to gain prudence, understanding, and instruction rather than silver or gold. Wisdom's delight was with the sons of men, and she calls them to listen. Those who hear and watch daily at her gates are blessed and find life, while those who sin against her wrong their own souls.

l: earth (creation), Proverbs, Chapter 8
s: The earth, along with the deeps, springs, mountains, hills, fields, and dust of the world, is described as not yet existing when wisdom was born. When the LORD established the heavens, set the sea's boundary so the waters would not violate his commandment, and marked out the earth's foundations, wisdom was present as craftsman by his side.
